title: ESG as Priced Crash Insurance: State-Dependent Tail Risk and Deconfounding Evidence

extraction.methodology_summary: The paper constructs a monthly firm-level panel of S&P 500 constituents from 2015 to 2025 using MSCI industry-adjusted ESG scores as the primary treatment variable. Market stress regimes are defined via a drawdown-based truncation rule classifying the bottom 15% of monthly market returns as stress periods. The authors evaluate the relationship between ESG and equity crashes using state-specific logit models, conditional quantile regressions across left-tail return quantiles, and Double Machine Learning (DML) with cross-fitting and Lasso or Random Forest estimators to control for high-dimensional firm-level confounders.
extraction.universe: U.S. equities constituents of the S&P 500 index

key_findings: High ESG ratings materially reduce the incidence of discrete equity crash events during systemic market drawdowns, but show no protective effect or even positive associations in non-stress regimes.
Conditional quantile regressions reveal that ESG protective effects are concentrated in the ultra-left tail of the return distribution rather than shifting the entire return distribution.
Double Machine Learning confirms an asymmetric treatment effect of ESG, acting as priced crash insurance rather than an unconditional alpha driver.
When decomposing pillar scores, the Social pillar acts as the primary resilience driver while the Environmental pillar represents insurance costs during stable periods.
